title: Reserved capacity prioritization, eviction and SLO mapping (PRD draft)
content:
Overview
This PRD defines behavior and configuration for tenant prioritization, eviction and SLO mapping within Reserved/Dedicated capacity. Focus is on predictable performance for paying tenants while allowing graceful burst/backfill, clear operator controls, and measurable business SLAs.

Background / problem
- Dedicated pools are sold as reserved throughput with burst allowances. Currently bursts are handled by naive first-come backfill and a global throttle when capacity saturates.
- Customers with different commitment tiers (bronze/silver/gold/enterprise) expect predictable latency and throughput. When capacity is tight, lower-tier workloads experience outages or long tail latency without predictable preemption semantics.
- Operators need safe, auditable controls to evict/backfill requests and to reconcile billing/credits when preemption occurs.

Goals (success criteria)
- Define priority classes and mapping from contractual tiers to runtime priority tokens.
- Create eviction semantics that are predictable and minimize customer-visible failures for higher-tier tenants.
- Provide config and API surface to express burst budgets, preemption thresholds, and grace windows per tenant/pool.
- Instrument metrics and logs needed to attribute preemptions and to reconcile billing/credits.
- Roll out with a canary phase on a subset of pools and a clear fallback path.

Non-goals
- This PRD does not redesign the serving runtime kernels or change model packing strategies. It focuses on allocation/prioritization and control plane behavior.

Key terms
- Reserved capacity: GPU capacity allocated to a customer under a commit.
- Burst allowance: Temporarily allowed extra throughput beyond reserved capacity, billed or free depending on contract.
- Priority token/class: Runtime label attached to each request used to make preemption/eviction decisions.
- Preemption: Termination or pause of an in-flight request or queued task to free capacity.

Design proposal
1) Priority classes
   - PRIORITY_ENTERPRISE (p0): Enterprise SLA, strict latency SLO, minimal preemption.
   - PRIORITY_STANDARD (p1): Committed customers with typical SLOs, allowed soft preemption.
   - PRIORITY_BURST (p2): Bursty workloads for short periods, allowed to be evicted when pool oversubscribed.
   - PRIORITY_LOW (p3): Backfill and best-effort workloads (e.g., internal testing); highest eviction likelihood.

   Mapping: product tier -> default priority class. Customer can opt into custom mappings via contract.

2) Reservation tokens and burst budgets
   - Each reservation includes: reserved_qps, burst_budget (tokens), burst_window_seconds, billing_mode (metered|covered).
   - Burst consumption reduces the burst_budget; when budget depleted, requests are either denied or demoted to lower priority depending on policy.

3) Eviction semantics
   - Soft eviction: request put into paused state with grace window (default 30s) to allow client retry or checkpoint. Not usable for streaming responses with no resumability.
   - Hard eviction: immediate termination and failure response. Used for long-running tasks and when operator explicitly triggers preemption.
   - Preemption order: p3 -> p2 -> p1 -> p0. Within a class, use oldest-queued-first (fairness) except where sticky reservations apply.
   - Eviction protection: small percentage (configurable, default 5%) of reserved slots per pool must remain non-preemptible for safety traffic (health checks, orchestration).

4) Graceful degradation and fallback
   - Automatic fallback to compatible model variants (quantized/cheaper) when preemption would otherwise impact higher-tier SLOs. Fallback only used if model variant is verified and configured for customer.
   - Allow routing policy that will split traffic across pools by priority to decrease eviction churn.

5) Operator controls & UI
   - Console: per-pool view for current utilization, per-tenant burst budget, active preemptions, and ability to pause preemptions for a tenant (admin override).
   - CLI: commands to set per-tenant priority, adjust burst budgets, and trigger controlled eviction drills.

6) API / config examples (text example)
   - Tenant reservation config (YAML-like):
       tenant_id: cust-123
       reserved_qps: 200
       burst_budget: 1_000_000_tokens
       burst_window_seconds: 86400
       billing_mode: metered
       default_priority: PRIORITY_STANDARD
       preemption_policy: soft-first

   - Runtime request header: X-Redwood-Priority: PRIORITY_BURST

7) Metrics & observability
   - reserved.capacity.utilization{pool,tenant} (gauge)
   - reserved.burst_used{tenant} (counter)
   - preemption.count{reason,from_priority,to_priority,tenant} (counter)
   - preemption.latency_impact{tenant} (histogram)
   - eviction.events{pool,tenant,policy,evict_type} (log stream)
   - billing.adjustments{tenant,period} (counter) for credits due to preempts

8) Billing & reconciliation
   - Preemption credit rule: if a request is hard-evicted after partially using resources beyond reserved quota, system calculates partial credit based on used tokens time-weighted; credit issued automatically as billing adjustment.
   - Burst-metering exporting: per-tenant burst_token_consumption exported hourly for finance reconciliation.

9) Safety nets and testing
   - Eviction dry-run mode: marks candidates for eviction but does not terminate; records metrics to predict user impact.
   - Canary rollout: enable on 5 pools that service non-critical tenants for 2 weeks, evaluate success metrics.

Rollout plan
- Phase 0 (2 weeks): implement telemetry and dry-run preemption in staging; basic console views.
- Phase 1 (4–6 weeks): enable soft preemption on canary pools; track preemption rates, SLO violation delta, and false positives.
- Phase 2 (6–8 weeks): enable hard preemption with billing credits on additional pools; provide customer opt-in controls.
- Phase 3 (ongoing): allow contract-level customization and propagate to Private deployments.

Open questions / trade-offs
- How to handle streaming/generative responses that cannot be safely paused? Proposal: use model-level labels to mark non-preemptible requests; require contract negotiation for non-preemptible reserved slots.
- Fairness vs business priority: within a priority class, should we prefer higher-paying tenants? Current proposal keeps fairness within class to avoid fragmentation and complexity.
- Complexity of billing: fine-grained credits increase accounting work—need to confirm finance acceptance of hourly export format.

Migration notes for existing customers
- Default behavior: newly enabled pools will map existing commitments to PRIORITY_STANDARD. Customers who previously experienced "silent failures" should be contacted and offered an entitlement review.
- Communication: email + console banner 30 days before enforcement of hard eviction. Provide a simulator where customers can test their burst profile and see expected preemption probability.

Appendix: acceptance criteria
- Less than 1% increase in p0 SLO violations after enabling soft preemption on canary pools.
- Automated credits calculated and exported for all hard preemption events during phase 2.
- Console shows per-tenant burst budget and consumed amount in near real-time (<= 30s delay).

Next steps / owners
- Priya Nair: prototype eviction dry-run + telemetry (2 sprints).
- Liam Chen: console mockups and admin override UX (1 sprint).
- Marisol Ortega: billing integration spec with finance (2 sprints).
- SRE: scheduling of canary pools and incident playbook updates.

Notes to self
- Need to sync with Serving Runtime team about tagging requests with model-compatibility for fallback.
- Keep simple for MVP: implement only PRIORITY_* mapping and soft eviction first.

Document history
- 2025-10-15: initial draft (Priya)
- 2025-10-22: added metrics and billing proposals (Marisol)
- 2025-11-02: updated rollout and added console controls (Liam)
